title: What is the Rosetta Stone? One message, three scripts
description: The Rosetta Stone helped unlock Egyptian hieroglyphs. Its secret was a message written three ways, with one version scholars could already read.

sections.title: A stone with a clue
sections.html:
The Rosetta Stone is a broken ancient Egyptian slab bearing a decree in three scripts. Comparing those versions helped scholars learn to read Egyptian hieroglyphs.

Its importance comes from the repeated message. Imagine finding the same unfamiliar notice beside a version you can understand: suddenly, you have something to work with.

sections.title: Three scripts, two languages
sections.html:
The British Museum dates the inscription to 196 BC. It concerns King Ptolemy V, rather than a secret map or a buried treasure.

The writing appears in Egyptian hieroglyphs, Egyptian Demotic and Ancient Greek. That means three scripts, but two languages: hieroglyphs and Demotic are different ways of writing Egyptian.

sections.title: The part they could read
sections.html:
Scholars could already read Ancient Greek. This gave them a route into the corresponding Egyptian text, including clues in royal names.

Progress still took years. Thomas Young made important advances, and Jean-François Champollion announced a crucial breakthrough in 1822. He worked with the stone and other texts; one glance at the Greek did not solve everything.

sections.title: A clue, not a magic key
sections.html:
That is what makes the story satisfying: familiar information helped make unfamiliar information readable. The stone supplied a comparison, and researchers did the difficult work.

For another shift in historical perspective, compare Cleopatra, the pyramids and the Moon landing. Or try reading a different system with Roman numerals.
